items.prompt: “Poor transport is the main problem limiting the development of tourism in Namibia.” How far do you agree with this statement?
items.canonical_answer: Partly agree. For the statement: attractions such as Etosha, Sossusvlei and Fish River Canyon are far apart and far from overseas markets; most roads are gravel or earth, so journeys are slow and costly; and the closure of Air Namibia in 2021 ended its own Frankfurt service, although other airlines continue direct international services. Against it: transport is only one constraint. Lodges also need capital for buildings, water and waste systems; marketing is needed to attract bookings; trained staff and good organisation are needed to deliver services; and seasonal demand leaves facilities underused. Decision: poor transport is a major problem, especially for remote sites, but it works together with capital, marketing and management problems, so it is not on its own the main problem.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for a judgement using Namibian transport evidence (distance, gravel roads, air links) weighed against other constraints (capital, marketing, organisation, seasonality).
1 C mark for a supported overall decision.

items.prompt: How far do you agree that a joint-venture lodge with a private investor is a good way for a community conservancy to overcome its lack of capital for tourism?
items.canonical_answer: Agree to a large extent. The investor supplies the money and management skills to build and run a lodge that the community could not finance itself, and the conservancy can receive contractual payments, jobs and training without taking on loans. However, benefits depend on the agreement: payments may be small or late, senior jobs may go to outsiders, profits can leave the area, and the community gives up some control over how its land is used. Decision: largely a good way, provided the contract sets fair payments, local jobs and training and is monitored so that members actually receive the benefits.
marking_guidance: Up to 4 C marks for a judgement using evidence that weighs the capital, skills, payment and job benefits against the risks of unfair or unfulfilled agreements, leakage and loss of control.

items.prompt:
A hypothetical lodge has 20 rooms available for ten nights. It sells 120 room-nights. It receives N$20,000 and pays N$8,000 to local workers/suppliers and N$7,000 outside the local area. Other obligations and final profit are unspecified.
(a) Name the outward spending flow from the assessed local economy. [1]
(b) Calculate room occupancy. [2]
(c) Describe three distinct capacity or spending features supported by the resource. [3]
(d) What judgement is supported about the claim “the remaining N$5,000 proves equal household benefit”? [1]
items.canonical_answer: (a) Leakage. (b) Available capacity is 20×10 = 200 room-nights; the occupied fraction is 120/200 = 0.6, equivalent to 60% occupancy. (c) Eighty room-nights are unsold; N$8,000 supports stated local payments; N$7,000 leaves the local boundary; N$5,000 remains before unspecified obligations. Credit three distinct supported features. (d) Reject the claim: a balance does not identify its distribution or establish equal household benefit.
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A mark for leakage.
(b) 2 B marks for the matched room-night method and 60% result.
(c) 3 B marks for three different patterns supported by resource evidence, without double-crediting occupancy and its equivalent unused share.
(d) 1 C mark for the supported distribution judgement.

(f) What conclusion about H1 is supported, including its evidence limit? [3]
(g) What conclusion about H2 is supported? [3]
(h) Design a fair test of the two stated hypotheses using the bi-polar grid. [3]
(i) Describe a usable site-selection and scoring procedure for the grid. [3]
(j) Complete the S3 total on the supplied results table. [2]
(k) Plot S1 and S5 on the provided axes. [2]
(l) Explain one limitation of surveying at a single time of day and a specific improvement. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Tertiary. (b) Relevant descriptions include litter, noise disturbance, trampled vegetation, crowding or pressure on facilities. (c) Accommodation laundry and guest washing, or two distinct suitable services. (d) Totals are −6, −3, +1, +5 and +8; mean (−6 − 3 + 1 + 5 + 8)/5 = +5/5 = +1 on the −10 to +10 scale. (e) Site totals rise steadily with distance, from −6 at 0 m to +8 at 400 m; litter, noise and crowding improve most, but facilities stay at +1 at every site. (f) H1 is supported for these five sites: the total rises at every step from −6 at 0 m to +8 at 400 m. The scores are observers' judgements from one half-hour survey of one path, so they do not prove that the car park alone causes the difference. (g) H2 is not supported: facilities score +1 at all five sites, so the rise in totals comes from the other rows. (h) Keep both hypotheses; place sites at equal intervals from the hot spot (systematic sampling); use the same five rows, scale and positive-left layout at every site; survey all sites at the same time of day and repeat on other days. (i) Choose rows that match the hypotheses; put every positive description on the same side; practise scoring together at one site; at each site, observe from a marked point for the same time, score every row, add the total and note anything unusual. (j) S3 row scores +1, 0, −1, 0 and +1 add to a total of +1. (k) Points (0, −6) and (400, +8). (l) Noise and crowding change through the day, so a 10:00 survey may not represent busy afternoons or weekends; repeat at several times and on a weekend day and compare. Other specific matched limitation/improvement pairs, such as observer judgement with two observers, are valid.

![S3 total completed as +1 and S1 and S5 plotted](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-2.3-P04-VIS-6137-2.3-01-answer.png)
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A mark for tertiary.
(b) 3 A marks for three different effect descriptions.
(c) 2 A marks for two distinct service names.
(d) 3 B marks for using the totals as data, the mean method and the answer +1 on the −10 to +10 scale.
(e) 3 B marks for the positive relationship with distance, evidence from the end sites and the constant facilities exception.
(f) 3 C marks for the H1 conclusion, paired evidence and the judgement/coverage limit.
(g) 3 C marks for the H2 conclusion, constant-score evidence and the total/component distinction.
(h) 3 D marks for a hypothesis test with systematic sampling at equal intervals, the same grid at every site and the same time of day.
(i) 3 D marks for choosing rows to match the hypotheses, positive descriptions on one side and a consistent scoring method.
(j) 2 D marks for correct use of the row data and the total +1.
(k) 2 D marks, one per correctly plotted point on the supplied axes.
(l) 2 D marks for a specific evaluation limitation (time of day) and an improvement addressing it.

items.prompt:
![Footpath stations every 30 m from a viewpoint car park, the measuring method, a record sheet with the S2 and S4 mean widths and S3 mean depth blank, and axes of mean width (0 to 250 cm) against distance (0 to 120 m) with S1, S3 and S5 plotted](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-2.3-P05-VIS-6137-2.3-02-question.png)

A teaching footpath investigation tests whether erosion decreases with distance from a viewpoint car park, the tourism hot spot. Stations S1 to S5 are placed every 30 m along the path, from 0 to 120 m. At each station, width is measured three times edge to edge with a tape at right angles to the path, and depth is the mean of five ruler readings below a pole laid across the path. Widths (cm): S1 215, 220, 225; S2 165, 170, 175; S3 130, 140, 150; S4 150, 155, 160; S5 90, 95, 100. Mean depths (cm): S1 8.0, S2 6.4, S4 3.0, S5 1.6; S3 readings 3.8, 4.4, 4.0, 4.6, 4.2. Field note: S4 lies in a wet, muddy hollow. H1: mean path width decreases at every station as distance from the car park increases. H2: mean path depth decreases as distance from the car park increases.
(a) Name the loss-and-movement process that can deepen an exposed path. [1]
(b) Describe three links from repeated unmanaged foot traffic to landscape damage. [3]
(c) Name two non-visitor influences on path form. [2]
(d) Calculate the mean depth at S3, including units. [3]
(e) Describe the width and depth patterns with distance, using an exception. [3]
(f) What conclusion about H1 is supported? [3]
(g) What conclusion about H2 and causation is supported? [3]
(h) Design a test using the two stated hypotheses. [3]
(i) Describe a consistent measurement and recording sequence. [3]
(j) Complete the mean-width entries for S2 and S4 on the supplied sheet. [2]
(k) Plot S2 and S4 on the provided axes. [2]
(l) Explain a limitation of sampling only five stations on one path and a specific improvement. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Erosion. (b) Trampling removes plant cover; bare, compacted ground lets runoff concentrate; flowing water and boots remove soil, widening and deepening the path. (c) Slope, surface material, drainage or rainfall: any two distinct factors. (d) (3.8 + 4.4 + 4.0 + 4.6 + 4.2)/5 = 21.0/5 = 4.2 cm. (e) Mean width falls from 220 cm at 0 m to 95 cm at 120 m, but rises from 140 cm at S3 to 155 cm at S4 in the wet hollow; mean depth falls at every station, from 8.0 to 1.6 cm. (f) H1 is not fully supported: width falls from S1 to S3 and from S4 to S5, but S4 (155 cm) is wider than S3 (140 cm), probably because walkers spread out around the mud. (g) H2 is supported: depth falls at each station from 8.0 cm to 1.6 cm. The survey compares distance with present path form; it does not measure visitor numbers, years of use or change over time, and slope, surface and drainage also vary, so it shows an association, not proof of cause. (h) Keep both hypotheses; place stations at equal intervals from the hot spot (systematic sampling); measure width and depth by the same method at every station; record slope, surface and drainage; repeat on a second path from the same car park. (i) At each station, define the edges, lay the tape at right angles and take three width readings; lay the pole across and take five equally spaced depth readings; record every reading in cm with notes, then calculate the means. (j) S2 (165 + 170 + 175)/3 = 170 cm; S4 (150 + 155 + 160)/3 = 155 cm. (k) Points (30, 170) and (90, 155). (l) Five stations 30 m apart on one path may miss changes between stations and may not represent other paths; place stations every 10 m and survey two more paths from the hot spot.

![S2 and S4 mean widths and S3 mean depth completed, and S2 and S4 plotted](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-2.3-P05-VIS-6137-2.3-02-answer.png)
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A mark for erosion.
(b) 3 A marks for three coherent landscape-effect descriptions.
(c) 2 A marks for two distinct relevant factor names.
(d) 3 B marks for using the five readings as data, the mean method and 4.2 cm with its unit.
(e) 3 B marks for the falling width pattern, the S4 exception as evidence and the steadily falling depth pattern.
(f) 3 C marks for the qualified H1 conclusion, the supporting falls and the contradicting S3 to S4 rise.
(g) 3 C marks for the H2 conclusion, depth evidence and the limit that distance does not itself measure visitor use or erosion through time.
(h) 3 D marks for a hypothesis test with systematic sampling at equal intervals, the same width/depth method and recorded site factors.
(i) 3 D marks for defined edges and tape orientation, repeated width and depth readings, and unit-labelled records.
(j) 2 D marks, one per completed mean.
(k) 2 D marks, one per correctly plotted point on the supplied axes.
(l) 2 D marks for the specific sampling limitation and an improvement addressing it (evaluation).

items.prompt:
![Summary form of yes and no responses for the quiet and busy periods with the busy denominator and both percentages blank, and blank bar-chart axes from 0 to 100 per cent](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-2.3-P06-VIS-6137-2.3-03-question.png)

A teaching survey compares matched quiet and busy periods. The same eligible group of twenty residents voluntarily answers yes or no in each period to the neutral question “During this period, did tourism improve your household income?” All twenty answer both times. Yes responses: quiet 12, busy 8. Matched ten-minute visitor counts: quiet 20, busy 60. H1: the share reporting an income benefit is higher in the busy period. H2: visitor counts are higher in the busy period. The supplied form records totals/denominators; provided bar-chart axes have period categories and percentages from 0 to 100.
(a) Name the direct benefit represented by wages from a guiding job. [1]
(b) Describe three possible disadvantages of seasonal tourism demand. [3]
(c) Name two different tourism-related services a visitor may use. [2]
(d) Calculate the quiet-period positive-response percentage. [3]
(e) Describe the response and visitor-count contrasts using values. [3]
(f) What conclusion about H1 is supported? [3]
(g) What conclusion about H2 and wider generalisation is supported? [3]
(h) Design a suitable test of the two stated hypotheses. [3]
(i) Describe an ethical selection, questioning and recording sequence. [3]
(j) Complete the busy-period percentage and its sample denominator on the supplied form. [2]
(k) Plot the two percentage bars on the provided axes. [2]
(l) Explain one limitation of the sample and a corresponding improvement. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Employment income. (b) Reduced quiet-season jobs/hours, underused capacity with continuing costs, or household income instability: three distinct relevant descriptions. (c) Guiding, accommodation, catering or transport: two distinct services. (d) The fraction is 12/20 = 0.6, equivalent to 60%. (e) Positive share falls from 60% to 40%, while visitor counts rise from 20 to 60; the resident-response denominator stays twenty in both periods. (f) H1 is rejected for the sample: the busy share is twenty percentage points lower, not higher. (g) H2 is supported by 60 versus 20; two matched observations do not establish the full year or all resident experiences. (h) State both predictions, record neutral responses from an appropriate resident sample and repeat matched visitor counts across the compared periods. (i) Define residents and a clear random/systematic/stratified selection rule, seek voluntary participation and record responses/non-response without identifying details. (j) Forty per cent; denominator twenty residents. (k) Quiet bar 60%, busy bar 40%. (l) Twenty selected residents may omit important groups or locations; broaden appropriate stratified coverage with a clear within-group rule, while retaining neutral questions and matched periods.

![Form completed (quiet 60%, busy 40%, denominator 20) and bars drawn](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-2.3-P06-VIS-6137-2.3-03-answer.png)
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A mark for employment income.
(b) 3 A marks for three distinct seasonal-cost point descriptions.
(c) 2 A marks for two service names.
(d) 3 B marks for percentage method, answer 60 and percent unit.
(e) 3 B marks for the response-share decline, visitor-count increase and stable sample denominator, each supported by data.
(f) 3 C marks for the H1 conclusion, paired share evidence and prediction-versus-result judgement.
(g) 3 C marks for the H2 conclusion, count evidence and coverage/generalisation limit.
(h) 3 D marks for hypothesis-linked resident evidence, matched count method and period design.
(i) 3 D marks for eligible selection, voluntary neutral questioning and usable anonymous recording.
(j) 2 D marks for the percentage and correct denominator.
(k) 2 D marks, one for each bar height on the supplied scale.
(l) 2 D marks for the specific sampling evaluation and a suitable coverage improvement.

items.prompt:
![Paired-site form for managed site M and reference site R with litter before and after and blank reduction cells, and visitor counts](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-2.3-P07-VIS-6137-2.3-01-question.png)

![Blank before-and-after axes for litter pieces from 0 to 25 with a key for sites M and R](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-2.3-P07-VIS-6137-2.3-04-question.png)

A teaching before-and-after investigation compares managed site M with reference site R over matched ten-minute periods. Litter pieces: M 20 before and 8 after; R 18 before and 16 after. Visitor counts at each site rise from 40 before to 80 after. A new bin/collection arrangement begins at M, but other influences are not fully controlled. H1: litter reduction is greater at M than R. H2: visitor counts fall after management begins. The supplied paired-site form has before/after columns; provided axes show before/after categories and litter pieces from 0 to 25, with a key for M/R.
(a) Name one waste pressure relevant to tourism. [1]
(b) Describe three functions of effective visitor-site management. [3]
(c) Name two other influences that should be recorded when comparing litter. [2]
(d) Calculate the percentage reduction in litter pieces at M. [3]
(e) Describe three distinct paired patterns using the data. [3]
(f) What conclusion about H1 and the management cause is supported? [3]
(g) What conclusion about H2 is supported? [3]
(h) Design a before-and-after test using the two hypotheses and a reference site. [3]
(i) Describe a consistent count and recording procedure. [3]
(j) Complete the absolute litter reductions for M and R on the supplied form. [2]
(k) Plot M’s before and after litter points on the provided axes. [2]
(l) Explain one specific limitation and a corresponding improvement. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Litter or a relevant named waste pressure. (b) Relevant functions include suitable waste collection, maintained paths/facilities, reliable responsibilities and monitoring. (c) Weather, general clean-up timing, other users or collection schedule: any two distinct relevant influences. (d) (20−8)/20×100 = 60%. (e) M falls twelve pieces while R falls two; both visitor counts double; M has less litter after despite more observed visitors. (f) H1 is supported by twelve versus two fewer pieces, but uncontrolled influences mean the bin arrangement alone is not established as the sole cause. (g) H2 is rejected: visitor counts rise from 40 to 80 at both sites. (h) State both predictions, retain a comparable reference and repeat matched before/after observations with relevant context. (i) Define count boundaries and pieces, use equal durations/areas, record raw totals and visitor counts before calculating changes. (j) M twelve pieces; R two pieces. (k) M before 20, after 8 on their respective categories. (l) An unmatched cleaning schedule could affect litter independently; match or record it and repeat observations across comparable periods.

![Litter reductions completed: M 12 pieces, R 2 pieces](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-2.3-P07-VIS-6137-2.3-01-answer.png)

![Site M plotted: 20 pieces before, 8 after](../../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-2.3-P07-VIS-6137-2.3-04-answer.png)
marking_guidance: (a) 1 A mark for a waste-pressure name.
(b) 3 A marks for three distinct management-function point descriptions.
(c) 2 A marks for two other-factor names.
(d) 3 B marks for reduction-over-original method, answer 60 and percent unit.
(e) 3 B marks for three distinct paired patterns supported by data.
(f) 3 C marks for the H1 conclusion, reference comparison and causal-attribution limit.
(g) 3 C marks for the H2 conclusion, paired count evidence and prediction/result distinction.
(h) 3 D marks for hypothesis-linked reference design, matched before/after timing and relevant control/context records.
(i) 3 D marks for operational definition, matched count method and usable records.
(j) 2 D marks, one for each absolute reduction.
(k) 2 D marks, one per correct point on the supplied axes and key.
(l) 2 D marks for the specific evaluation limitation and a matched improvement.
